newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dlr support buckles, crucial test looms.
newsitem.headline: Australian dlr support buckles, crucial test looms.

text.p: The Australian dollar delved beneath 76 cents to three month lows Monday as exporter support finally buckled beneath the burden of offshore selling.

Traders said disappearing interest differentials were the driving force as the surprise cut in official rates a fortnight ago and fears another may be in the pipeline, gifted the U.S. dollar with better investment returns.

Overseas funds, led by big-name New York investment houses, were trimming their A$ exposure as a result and the pressure looked likely to soon have the currency testing its 1997 trough of US$0.7550, beneath which 16-month lows beckoned.
By 5.00 pm (0700 GMT) the dollar had bowed to US$0.7580/85, its second lowest finish this year after the US$0.7558/63 from February 12.
It opened under fire at US$0.7599/04 having failed to recoup any of the losses suffered in Friday's slide from US$0.7680.

The currency has now lost almost two cents since the Reserve Bank sprang its last surprise rate cut on the market on May 23 and more than six cents since it peaked atop 82 cents in December prior to the RBA's, then, third easing.
The latest setback was triggered by dire retail sales data which had the market taking bets on a fifth move.
The 1.7 percent drop in April sales confounded expectations of a healthy rise and forced analysts to reconsider the previously accepted view the economy would recover robustly in 1997.
That in turn opened up the startling prospect of yet another cut in official interest rates, the fifth since the easing cycle began in July last year.

The bank's policy board holds its monthly meeting on Tuesday and could well grant the governor authority to ease should he deem it necesary. But most analysts doubted he would do so immediately given the proximity of the May 23 cut.

"It seems highly unlikely the RBA would ease rates within tweo weeks of the last adjustment -- to do so would reek of panic over the economic outlook," said Glenn Maguire, an economist at Societe Generale Australia.

"However, the recent strong of weak foreward looking data strongly suggests the RBA must still have an easing bias," he added. If the run of data remained soft an easing was on the cards, possibly after the bank's next board meeting on July 1.
Such has been the market's descent into gloom that today's building approvals data were all but ignored despite providing confirmation the housing sector was enjoying a recovery.
Approvals rose 3.6 percent in April to more than compensate for a 1.8 percent dip the month before.
Crucially approvals for private sector houses, long considered a bellweather of housing market health, jumped 11 percent for the highest monthly total since February 1995.
Formerly, growth had largely been confined to the volatile multi-unit sector, so analysts were encouraged to see house building winning a share.
"The key feature of today's figures were indications the housing recovery is broadening out," said Michael Blythe, an economist at Commonwealth Bank.
"They should dispel some of the gloom that energed after the retail trade numbers," said Blythe.
But added, "An upturn in housing has been part of the script for 1997 for some time so there is little in the way of policy implications...the risks remain skewed toward another easing."

The extent of the risk may be easier to assess after March quarter GDP data are released on Wednesday. Analysts have had to nudge down their forecasts recently and estimates of growth now range from 1.2 percent to as little as 0.25 percent.
Those results would give annual growth of between 2.5 and 1.75 percent, down from 3.1 percent in Q4 last year.
On the crosses the currency was relegated to the sidelines as the market pondered the implications of a shock left wing victory in the French general election.

The main opposition Socialist party won the most seats but will need the support of the Communists to rule, leaving analysts more concerned than ever that France will seek to loosen the tough criteria of European monetary union.

The risk of having the hard mark swapped for a soft single currency saw the German unit marked down on the U.S. dollar and even the A$ managed a modest rise to 1.2989/02 marks from 1.2941/53 late Friday.
